passage: Noor, you asked why my portfolio has a shop sheet in it instead of another clone, so listen, I'm Abhinav. I was about to build my fifth tutorial app when I walked past Sharma Stores, the family shop near my hostel. The owner keeps stock in a notebook and runs out of things without noticing. I offered to build something. He said, "As long as it's simple." That word, simple, shaped everything. He does not use a laptop, only a phone. So I built a small sheet with three columns and a colour that turns red when stock is low. I sat there while he tried it and he got confused by one button, which I changed the same day. Now I have a story to tell an interviewer, and a real person who uses it.

passage:
I'm Lakshmi. My family runs a stationery shop at the corner of our lane in Hyderabad, and Afreen from the second floor studies computer science.
Last summer she stood at our counter while my father searched, for the third time, for a box of blue pens he swore we had. She said, half to herself, 'Everyone in my class is building weather apps. Nobody will remember a weather app. But this shop has a real problem.'
She asked if she could make something. Not an app, just a sheet on our old laptop: item, shelf, how many left, when to reorder. She came every evening for a week, asking my father things like 'What runs out first before exams?' and changing the sheet each time.
Now my father types in sales at closing. Last month Afreen told me an interviewer spent twenty minutes asking about our pens.

qa.q: Which columns did Afreen's sheet have?
qa.a: Item, shelf, how many left, when to reorder.

qa.q: What does Afreen's remark at the counter suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: She seems restless about building one more forgettable clone and excited to find a real problem with a real user right in front of her.

qa.q: What else could Afreen add to the project story for interviews?
qa.a: A short note on what changed for the shop, such as fewer lost items before exams, so the story shows a result.

qa.q: How does the project look to Lakshmi's father?
qa.a: For him it ends the searching for lost boxes, and typing in sales at closing becomes a small habit that helps the shop.

grounding: Shows a student choosing to build a stock sheet for a nearby family shop instead of a clone, gaining a real user, real limits and a story for interviews.

subtype: Approach: solving a real local problem [Thinking]
passage:
Monday, early June. Nitin's portfolio has two tutorial clones and an empty third slot. Walking past his uncle Manoj's hardware shop in Nagpur, he watches Manoj flip through a thick register to check whether any 12 mm bolts are left. Nitin thinks: that's a real problem, and a real person I can ask.
Thursday, two weeks later. Nitin's first sheet is too complicated. Manoj can't type fast at the counter, and he calls the drop-down menus 'a puzzle'. Nitin cuts the sheet to four columns and adds big buttons for the ten items that sell most.
Saturday, end of July. Manoj checks the bolts in five seconds. At a campus interview, Nitin is asked about his projects and talks for ten minutes about a shop counter, a slow typist and ten big buttons. The interviewer keeps writing.

qa.q: What did Manoj call the drop-down menus?
Why did Nitin choose the shop over another clone, and how was he feeling about it?
qa.a: He was curious and motivated, seeing a real problem and a real person he could ask, instead of a third tutorial copy.

qa.q: What would you advise Nitin to do next with the sheet?
qa.a: Check with Manoj after a month which buttons get used and which do not, so the tool keeps fitting the counter.

qa.q: How might Manoj see his nephew's project?
qa.a: For Manoj it saves time and frustration at the counter, once the sheet became simple enough for a slow typist.

grounding: Shows a student building a stock sheet for an uncle's hardware shop, meeting real limits, and gaining a story for interviews.
